privacy.charterSubtitle: How PMSify handles your information, and where the boundaries between its three systems sit.
privacy.localStorageBody: Your personal health logs, period dates, symptoms, and notes are stored privately and locally on this device. No cloud telemetry or automatic cloud backups are performed for your tracking data.
privacy.offlineNotice: Your tracking logs are stored 100% locally on this device.
privacy.guaranteeNoCloudSync: Period dates, daily health logs, and notes are never uploaded. They exist only in this browser's local storage.
privacy.guaranteeNoTelemetry: PMSify does not send analytics, tracking, or usage data anywhere.
privacy.guaranteeExport: You can export or erase everything PMSify holds, at any time, from Settings.
privacy.pinLockTitle: The local PIN is a privacy lock, not security
privacy.pinLockBody: Your PIN is never stored. PMSify keeps only a salted hash, in the same local database as your records. This deters someone casually opening PMSify on a shared or borrowed device. It does not protect you from a person with access to your browser's developer tools, and it is not a substitute for a device passcode.
privacy.pinLockRecoveryBody: There is no PIN recovery. PMSify stores no email address, phone number, or account, so it has nothing that could identify you in order to reset it. A forgotten PIN can only be resolved by erasing all local data and starting again.
privacy.separationTitle: How the three systems stay separate
privacy.separationBody: PMSify has three systems with different rules. Keeping them separate is a design constraint, not a policy statement.
privacy.separationLocalToCommunity: Nothing from your personal tracker is ever published to SecretChat. You choose each post yourself, and you type it yourself.
privacy.separationCommunityToHealthcare: Your SecretChat identity and activity are not visible to ASHA workers, doctors, or anyone in the healthcare portals.
privacy.separationLocalToHealthcare: A healthcare worker cannot see your local tracking data. Sharing a summary with a clinician is an action you take deliberately, and it is a separate copy — not a live link to this device.

cyclePhases.title: What the four phases of your cycle are
cyclePhases.summary: Your cycle is not one event but four repeating phases, and each one tends to feel different.
cyclePhases.body: Menstruation is the phase where the uterine lining is shed, usually lasting a few days. Immediately after it, the follicular phase begins: rising oestrogen rebuilds the lining and energy and mood often lift. Somewhere in this phase, the pituitary gland releases luteinising hormone and an egg is released from an ovary — that is ovulation. After ovulation, the luteal phase runs until your next period, driven mainly by progesterone. Many people notice the most distinct physical and emotional changes during the luteal phase. || None of these phases lasts exactly the same number of days every time, and a phase that feels different from one cycle to the next is not automatically a problem. PMSify records your actual dates and works out your own pattern, rather than assuming a standard 28-day template.

fertileWindow.title: What the fertile window means, and what it does not
fertileWindow.summary: The fertile window is a calculated estimate, not a guarantee, and it is not a contraceptive method.
fertileWindow.body: The fertile window is the span of days when pregnancy is considered more likely, based on when ovulation is estimated to occur and how long sperm and an egg can survive. PMSify estimates it from your own recorded cycle lengths, using fixed arithmetic — not by observing your body. || Because the estimate is only as good as the assumption that your cycles repeat, it will drift for anyone whose cycle length varies. It also cannot detect ovulation itself. Timing intercourse to avoid pregnancy using this estimate is not safe, because real ovulation can happen earlier or later than predicted. || If you are planning a pregnancy or avoiding one, please speak to a doctor or a qualified family-planning service about methods that do not depend on predicting a single day.

pmsVsPmd.title: PMS and PMDD: what is the difference
pmsVsPmd.summary: Premenstrual symptoms are common. PMDD is a much more severe medical condition and is not simply 'bad PMS'.
pmsVsPmd.body: PMS covers a wide range of physical and emotional symptoms in the one to two weeks before a period, which settle once bleeding starts. Common ones include bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, cravings, and feeling irritable or low. PMS is treatable and many people find it manageable. || PMDD, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, is different in both severity and cause. Symptoms are severe enough to disrupt work, study, or relationships, and they are present for most cycles, not occasionally. PMDD is diagnosed by a clinician using a symptom diary recorded across at least two cycles. It can respond to treatments that ordinary PMS does not. || A useful reason to keep tracking: PMSify records your symptoms day by day, so if you and a doctor are trying to work out whether what you experience is PMS or something else, you will arrive with records rather than guesses.

painTracking.title: Tracking pain, and when to stop tracking and see someone
painTracking.summary: Logging pain on a simple 0–10 scale turns 'it hurt a lot' into something a clinician can actually use.
painTracking.body: A pain score is subjective, which is exactly why a repeated series of scores is useful. One number alone means little; a trend across several cycles tells you whether your pain is changing. PMSify asks for a 0–10 number alongside the symptom names you select, so the record shows both what hurt and how much. || Record the timing as well as the number. Pain that builds steadily over several days and then eases with bleeding is a common pattern. Pain that starts well before bleeding and continues for days after it ends is a different pattern, and worth mentioning to a doctor. || Some pain is not something to wait out. Seek medical care promptly if the pain is severe and sudden, comes with fever, fainting, heavy or prolonged bleeding, pain during pregnancy, or pain that is getting steadily worse. You do not need to justify that — severe pain is a reason to be seen, not to be reassured.

sleepStressCycle.title: Sleep, stress, and how they interact with your cycle
sleepStressCycle.summary: Sleep and stress do not sit apart from your cycle; they tend to move with it.
sleepStressCycle.body: Poor sleep and high stress commonly cluster in the luteal phase, the stretch after ovulation and before your next period. That is not a personal failing — it is a pattern many people notice. Hormonal changes in this phase can make sleep feel lighter and make stress feel harder to manage. || Poor sleep also affects what you can tolerate. Fatigue and low mood make pain feel worse and cravings more intense, which can turn a manageable cycle into a difficult one. The practical lever is usually consistency of sleep and wake time rather than total hours, especially around the days before a period. || If you are sleeping poorly for weeks at a time regardless of where you are in your cycle, or if you feel unable to cope with everyday demands, that is worth raising with a doctor rather than treating as a PMS symptom to endure.

hydrationEnergy.title: Hydration, energy, and what to drink
hydrationEnergy.summary: Water intake is one of the simplest things to record, and small changes are easier to sustain than big ones.
hydrationEnergy.body: Hydration is worth tracking because it is directly measurable and directly changeable. Many people find their intake is lower on days they are busy or travelling, which is often also when their symptoms are worse. PMSify records millilitres so you can see the shape of your week rather than a single total. || Water is the safest default. Caffeine, strong tea, and alcohol all have real effects on sleep, and because sleep already tends to be disrupted before a period, reducing them around that window is a low-risk change many people find worthwhile. || A note on energy drinks and supplements: some interact with prescribed medicines, and supplement claims are often not well tested. Check with a doctor or pharmacist before starting any supplement, especially if you take regular medication.

pcosOverview.title: PCOS: what it is and how it is diagnosed
pcosOverview.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is one of the most common conditions affecting periods — and it can take years to diagnose.
pcosOverview.body: PCOS is a hormonal and metabolic condition, not a gynaecological cosmetic issue. It is associated with irregular or infrequent periods, signs of androgen excess such as acne or excess hair, difficulty conceiving, and in some cases insulin resistance. It is also strongly associated with metabolic health, including type 2 diabetes risk, which is why assessment is not only about periods. || Diagnosis is made by a clinician using a defined set of criteria — typically a combination of menstrual pattern, blood tests, and sometimes an ultrasound — and other causes have to be ruled out first. It is frequently missed in younger women, in lean women, and in women whose symptoms are treated as simply stressful. || Nothing you track on your own can confirm or rule out PCOS. What tracking does give you is a precise history: how many days between periods, what pattern over how many months, and how the numbers have changed. That history is often the thing that finally moves a diagnosis forward.

anaemiaFatigue.title: Anaemia, fatigue, and why they are easy to miss
anaemiaFatigue.summary: Persistent tiredness is often blamed on stress or hormones. Sometimes it is low iron, and that is testable.
anaemiaFatigue.body: Iron-deficiency anaemia is common in women, and it is frequently mistaken for tiredness, stress, or a difficult phase of the cycle. Common signs include fatigue that does not lift with rest, breathlessness on stairs, palpitations, headaches, dizziness, pale skin, and brittle nails. Heavy or prolonged periods are one of the main causes, and PMSify records flow intensity and duration, which gives a clinician a way to judge whether your losses are unusually heavy. || Anaemia is diagnosed with a simple blood test, not by how you feel. It is also treatable. What is not advisable is self-prescribing iron supplements, because iron overload is harmful and some causes of anaemia need different treatment. || If you are tired all the time and it has lasted more than a few weeks, ask a doctor for a blood test rather than adjusting your habits and hoping.

endometriosisOverview.title: Endometriosis: what it is, and why it is so often missed
endometriosisOverview.summary: Severe period pain is routinely blamed on being normal. Endometriosis is a real, treatable condition, and the average diagnosis takes years.
endometriosisOverview.body: Endometriosis is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, the fallopian tubes, or the lining of the pelvis. This tissue still responds to the menstrual cycle, so it tends to bleed and swell with each period in a place where the blood has no way out. That is what causes the inflammation, the adhesions, and the pain. It is not a lifestyle problem, and it is not caused by anything you have done. Prevalence estimates vary widely between studies, but it is commonly reported in around one in ten women of reproductive age, and a large share of them have never been diagnosed. || The pattern that raises suspicion is distinctive: period pain severe enough to stop normal daily activity, pain that worsens over the years rather than settling, pain during or after sex, pain when passing urine or opening your bowels around period time, heavy or prolonged bleeding, and difficulty conceiving. None of these symptoms is unique to endometriosis. They overlap heavily with adenomyosis, fibroids, ovarian cysts, pelvic infection, and irritable bowel syndrome, and telling them apart is a clinician’s job rather than an app’s. What PMSify can show is the pattern across time: how many days between periods, how heavy each period was, and how those numbers have changed. A clear history like that is often what makes a referral easier to act on. || Diagnosis cannot be made by an app, a symptom diary, or a routine blood test. It usually takes a combination of clinical history, an examination, and imaging, and sometimes a laparoscopy, and it is regularly missed or delayed for years, particularly in women whose pain was put down to ordinary menstrual cramps. Nothing you track in PMSify can confirm or rule out endometriosis, and this article does not suggest that you have it. Please seek medical care rather than managing it alone if your periods are painful enough to stop you working or studying, if the pain is getting worse, if you have had heavy bleeding across several cycles, if sex is painful, or if you have been trying to conceive for a year without success.

whenToSeeDoctor.title: Symptoms that deserve a doctor's attention
whenToSeeDoctor.summary: Some changes are worth investigating on their own, without waiting to see whether they repeat.
whenToSeeDoctor.body: It is reasonable to seek medical advice rather than continue tracking when you notice: periods that have stopped for three months or more without a pregnancy; cycles that have become much shorter, much longer, or far more irregular than your own previous pattern; bleeding that soaks through protection hourly or lasts far longer than your usual; severe pain that is new, worsening, or not eased by ordinary measures; pain during sex; or bleeding after menopause. || Seek prompt care, rather than a routine appointment, for severe or sudden pelvic pain, pain with fever or vomiting, fainting, or heavy bleeding, and always for any possibility of pregnancy with pain or bleeding. || None of this means a symptom is serious. It means the question is answerable, and answering it early is easier than answering it late. A doctor cannot diagnose you over an app, and this page is not a diagnosis — it is a list of reasons not to delay a conversation you have been putting off.

talkingToDoctor.title: Getting your concerns taken seriously
talkingToDoctor.summary: The way you raise a health concern has a measurable effect on what you are offered. This is about preparation, not assertiveness alone.
talkingToDoctor.body: Bring a record. Dates, a symptom list, a pain score series, and a note of what you have already tried are far more useful than a description from memory, because they turn a general worry into a specific question. PMSify's Insights and Reports screens are designed to be read out loud in a consultation. || State the main concern in your first sentence. A clinician will otherwise decide what the problem is based on the first thing you mention. You can also say plainly that you have looked into the cause and what you are asking for. || If you are told something is nothing and you disagree, it is legitimate to ask what would need to be different for it to be investigated, and to ask whether a follow-up or a second opinion is appropriate. If you have felt dismissed before, say that too — it is useful information, and you can ask for a doctor who works with women, or bring someone with you for support.

responses.greeting: Hello. I can explain your cycle, what you have recorded, and the health information in our education library. What would you like to know?
responses.crisisRefusal: I am not able to help with this, and I do not want to leave you to handle it alone. Please speak to a health professional or call one of the numbers above today. If you are in immediate danger, please call emergency services.
responses.diagnosisRefusal: I cannot tell you whether you have a condition, and a guess from me could do real harm. What your records can show is a pattern worth taking to a doctor, who can give you a proper answer. Please book a consultation.
responses.medicationRefusal: I cannot advise on medicines, doses or supplements, because getting that wrong is genuinely dangerous. Please take that question to a doctor or a pharmacist.
responses.outOfScopeRefusal: I only answer questions about women's health, so that is not something I can help with.
responses.noMatch: I can help with how PMSify works, with the cycle and health information you have recorded here, with women’s health questions in general, and with knowing when a symptom is worth seeing a doctor about. I could not answer that particular question from what I know, so try different words, or browse the education library yourself.
responses.predictionReady: From the cycles you have recorded, your next period is estimated to start around {estimatedDate}. This is calculated from your own records, so please treat it as an estimate rather than a certainty.
responses.predictionWithWindow: From the cycles you have recorded, your next period is estimated to start around {estimatedDate}, and your estimated fertile window is {windowStart} to {windowEnd}. Both are calculated from your records, so please treat them as estimates.
responses.predictionInsufficient: I cannot estimate that yet. It takes at least two completed cycles, and you currently have {recordedCycles}. Log one more cycle and the estimate will appear here and on your calendar.
responses.noData: There is not enough recorded yet for me to say anything about dates.
responses.summaryNoData: You have not recorded anything yet. Once you log a period or a daily health entry, I can summarise what is there.
responses.summaryWithCycle: You have recorded {recordedCycles} cycles and {recordedDays} daily entries. Your average cycle is {averageCycle} days and your average period is {averagePeriod} days.
responses.summaryNoCycle: You have recorded {recordedCycles} cycles and {recordedDays} daily entries. There is not yet enough recorded to calculate an average cycle length.
responses.education: Here is what our education library says, from {count, plural, =1 {# article} other {# articles}}.

log.answer: Tap "Log period" on the Daily & Period screen and enter the start date of your period.
log.detail: You can also add the end date and how heavy the flow was. A period you have already logged can be edited or removed from the same screen, and the rest of the app is built from these entries, so logging them even roughly makes the rest of it more useful.

daily.answer: The daily check-in is on the same Daily & Period screen, above the period section.
daily.detail: Each day you can record sleep, water, mood, symptoms, pain and a private note. Your insights and predictions are calculated from these entries, so a day you skip is simply a day the app cannot learn from.

predictions.answer: Your estimated period dates, your fertile window and your estimated ovulation day are on the Home screen.
predictions.detail: PMSify works them out from the cycles you have recorded, so they appear once there are enough completed cycles. The Calendar deliberately shows recorded facts only, which is why the estimates are not on it.

cycleDay.answer: Cycle day is the count of days since the first day of your last period, with that first day counted as day 1. It resets each time a new period starts, and PMSify uses it to describe which part of your cycle you are in.

calendar.answer: The Calendar shows the days you have actually recorded, with the cycle day for each of them. It does not show predicted dates, so it fills in only as you log.

insights.answer: Patterns across everything you have recorded are on the Insights screen.

reports.answer: Reports gather what you have logged into one place for a date range you choose, ready to show a doctor.

exportData.answer: You can export your data from the Reports screen, which produces a file you can save or send on.
exportData.detail: A report can be exported as PDF, CSV or JSON, and Settings has a separate option to export everything the app holds. Both work offline, and the file goes wherever you choose to put it.

eraseData.answer: Settings has an option to erase all local data. It removes your cycles, your daily logs and your PIN from this device, and it cannot be undone.

privacy.answer: Your cycle records, your daily entries and your PIN are stored on this device only. The tracker has no account, and nothing in it is uploaded unless you deliberately switch on the optional online assistant.
privacy.detail: Your PIN is stored as a salted hash rather than as text, so it cannot be read back. The tracker, SecretChat and the healthcare portals are three separate systems: posting in SecretChat does not give anyone access to your health log, and the healthcare portals ask for their own sign-in.

secretChat.answer: SecretChat is a separate community space. Posts there are anonymous, and it cannot read your health log or show your name.
secretChat.detail: It needs its own sign-in, and because it is a separate system it only works once it is connected to a server. It is not connected in this build, so posting is unavailable.

reminders.answer: Reminders are set on the Reminders screen, where you can choose a period expectation reminder and a daily check-in reminder.
reminders.detail: They are local notifications, so they appear only while PMSify is open in a browser tab. A closed app, or a phone with the browser closed, will not remind you.

settings.answer: Settings holds your PIN, your data export and erase options, and an explanation of how the app calculates things. The language selector is in the app header at the top, not in Settings.

healthcare.answer: PMSify also has separate signed-in portals for ASHA health workers, doctors and health camps. They are a different system from the tracker and ask you to sign in again.
healthcare.detail: Signing in to a portal does not connect it to your personal cycle records and does not change anything in the tracker. Health camps can be browsed without signing in.

education.answer: The Education section is a library of short articles on menstrual health, symptoms and when to see a doctor. When an answer comes from one of those articles, it tells you which one was used.

assistantScope.answer: PMSify can tell you what it has worked out from your own records: your cycle day and the phase you are in, your average cycle and period length, your estimated dates, your most common symptoms and moods, and the insights drawn from them.
assistantScope.detail: It cannot see the notes you write, it cannot diagnose anything, and it cannot advise you on medicines. It also cannot invent a number: if an estimate would need more cycles than you have recorded, it says so instead of guessing.

menstruation.answer: A period, or menstruation, is the shedding of the uterine lining when a pregnancy has not happened. It is one stage of the menstrual cycle, which runs from the first day of a period to the day before the next one starts.
menstruation.detail: The cycle moves through phases across the month, and understanding those phases is what explains why your symptoms, energy and mood change at different points in it.

cycleLength.answer: A cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the day before the next, so its length includes the days of bleeding. Not everybody has a 28-day cycle, and the same person can have different lengths from cycle to cycle.
cycleLength.detail: Cycle length normally shortens and varies through life, so a change in your own pattern is worth more attention than any number printed on a chart.

periodDuration.answer: How many days a period lasts varies between people and from month to month. It does not have to be the same length every time.

spotting.answer: Spotting is a small amount of bleeding or staining between periods, or after a period has finished. It is often dark brown or pink, because old blood has had time to change colour.
spotting.detail: It can also appear as ovulation happens, and light staining is common during the first few cycles. Hormonal contraception is another frequent reason for it.
spotting.warning: Spotting is worth checking if it keeps happening, if it is new, if it comes after sex, or if it comes with pain or a fever.

heavyBleeding.answer: Heavy bleeding is when you soak a pad or a tampon every hour for more than an hour at a time, pass clots larger than a coin, or have to get up more than once in a night to change.
heavyBleeding.detail: Over time it can cause anaemia, which shows up as tiredness, breathlessness and feeling light-headed. That is worth treating rather than living with.
heavyBleeding.warning: Soaking through protection every hour, or bleeding along with dizziness, weakness or fainting, needs medical attention the same day.
heavyBleeding.care: A doctor can check for anaemia with a blood test and look into why the bleeding is heavy. There are treatments that reduce it, and this is not something to manage on your own.

irregularPeriods.answer: Periods are called irregular when the time between them keeps changing, or when bleeding comes more often or less often than your own usual pattern. It is a description of a pattern, not a diagnosis.
irregularPeriods.detail: Common reasons include stress, illness, a change in routine, a change in body weight, a lot of exercise, and menopause. Cycles are often irregular to begin with in the first few years after periods start.
irregularPeriods.warning: Periods that are very far apart, that stop for months, or that become irregular alongside very heavy bleeding or severe pain should be checked by a doctor.

missedPeriod.answer: A period can be delayed by many ordinary things: stress, illness, travel, a change in routine, or a change in body weight. The cycle is sensitive to how much energy you use and how you sleep.
missedPeriod.detail: Pregnancy is the first thing to check if a period is late and pregnancy is possible, and a home pregnancy test can answer that quickly. If you are not pregnant and your cycles stay irregular, that is worth mentioning to a doctor.
missedPeriod.warning: Seek care if a period is several months late, if you have missed three or more in a row, or if you feel unwell alongside the delay.

cramps.answer: Period cramps come from the uterus contracting to shed its lining, and from reduced blood flow to it during the first day or two. Prostaglandins, the hormones that trigger those contractions, are what make the pain feel intense.
cramps.detail: Cramps that build up over months can have a cause other than ordinary cramps, including endometriosis, fibroids and adenomyosis. Being told that severe pain is simply something to endure is not the only option.
cramps.warning: Cramps with a fever, cramps with vomiting, one-sided pain, fainting, or pain so severe you cannot move or work need medical attention.

pms.answer: PMS, premenstrual syndrome, is the set of symptoms that arrive in the days before a period and settle once it starts. It is driven by the hormone changes of the cycle rather than by the bleeding itself.
pms.detail: Common symptoms include tiredness, bloating, breast tenderness, mood swings, irritability and food cravings. They usually ease once the bleeding begins.

pmdd.answer: PMDD, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, is a severe form of premenstrual symptoms that disrupts daily life. It is a recognised condition, not an exaggeration.
pmdd.detail: It is diagnosed by tracking symptoms across several cycles, because what matters is not how you feel once but how consistently it happens before periods and clears afterwards.
pmdd.care: Severe premenstrual symptoms are treatable, with hormonal, non-hormonal and psychological options. A doctor or a mental health professional can help you work out which fits.

menstrualHygiene.answer: Menstrual hygiene is staying comfortable and healthy while bleeding: changing pads, tampons or cups regularly, washing with water rather than douching, and keeping whatever you use dry between changes.
menstrualHygiene.detail: Change protection on the schedule your own flow needs rather than by a fixed rule for everyone, and wash your hands before and after. Tampons are not risk-free if left in far longer than their time limit, so follow the pack.

menstrualFatigue.answer: Feeling tired before or during a period is common and usually has more than one reason: broken sleep from cramps, a dip in iron before a period, the hormone changes themselves, or less sleep and less activity than usual.
menstrualFatigue.detail: If it is new, if it is getting worse, or if it is there even between periods, it is worth thinking about the other common causes rather than assuming it is only your cycle.
menstrualFatigue.care: Iron deficiency is the first thing worth ruling out, and a simple blood test can do that. If the tiredness does not lift after resting, or it comes with breathlessness or dizziness, a doctor can look into it.

vulva.answer: The vulva is the outside of the genitals: the outer and inner lips, the clitoris, the openings of the urethra and the vagina, and the surrounding skin.
vulva.detail: Vulva and vagina are different parts, and the two words get mixed up constantly. The vulva is outside; the vagina is inside.

vagina.answer: The vagina is the muscular canal inside the body that connects the outer opening to the cervix. Its walls rest against each other rather than being held open.
vagina.detail: It expands for birth, and it cleans itself, so it does not need cleaning inside with soap or antiseptics, which tend to irritate it.
vagina.warning: Discharge that is new, smells strong, comes with itching or soreness, or comes with pain when you pass urine is worth having checked rather than treated at home.

vaginaOpening.answer: The vaginal opening is the entrance at the inner end of the vulva, the part the labia surround. It stretches, so it can change shape and size.

cervix.answer: The cervix is the lower, narrow part of the uterus, opening into the vagina. It produces cervical mucus, which changes through the cycle and helps sperm reach the egg when a pregnancy is possible.
cervix.detail: That mucus becomes thinner and slippery around ovulation and thicker at other times, which is part of how the fertile window is worked out. The cervix itself also opens slightly and sits a little higher around ovulation, which some people track.

uterus.answer: The uterus, or womb, is the muscular organ a baby develops in. It has an inner lining called the endometrium, which thickens each cycle and is shed as a period when a pregnancy does not happen.
uterus.detail: The uterine muscle is what makes period cramps feel strong, because it contracts to shed that lining. It also opens and contracts during labour.

fallopianTubes.answer: The fallopian tubes connect the ovaries to the uterus. One of them carries the egg along after ovulation, and that is where fertilisation usually happens.

ovaries.answer: The ovaries are two small organs that store and release eggs and produce hormones, including oestrogen, progesterone and testosterone. Usually one egg is released in a cycle.
ovaries.detail: They sit on either side of the uterus, and the number of eggs they hold is set before birth and declines over the years.

puberty.answer: Puberty is the stage of development when the body changes from a child's into an adult's. It brings growth in height, changes in body shape, breast development, periods, and new hair in certain areas.
puberty.detail: It happens over several years rather than all at once, and everybody's timing is different. Some changes arrive earlier in puberty and others later, which is why people the same age can look quite different from each other.

firstPeriod.answer: Your first period is called menarche. It is a normal part of growing up, and for most people it happens somewhere between about 8 and 15.
firstPeriod.detail: The first few cycles are often irregular, and can be lighter, heavier or more painful than they settle into later. Period pain is common at first and often improves with age.
firstPeriod.warning: Get advice if the bleeding is heavy enough to soak protection every hour for hours, if it lasts longer than about a week, if periods have not started by around 15, or if there is severe pain.

irregularFirstCycles.answer: Periods are often irregular for the first few years after they start, and it is common to have long gaps between them or cycles that change from month to month.
irregularFirstCycles.detail: It happens because the cycle is still settling, and it often settles down on its own without any treatment.
irregularFirstCycles.care: It is worth talking to a doctor if periods have not started by around 15, if they stop for more than three months at a time, if they are extremely heavy or painful, or if it is causing distress. Keeping a record of your cycle length helps a doctor a lot.

consent.answer: Consent means that both people freely agree to something, and that either of them can say no or change their mind at any time, including after saying yes at the start.
consent.detail: It has to be agreement in the moment, and it has to be a real choice. Not saying no is not the same as saying yes, and pressure, fear, being drunk, or being someone older all take away a genuine yes. It applies to everything from touching to sex, and it can be given again for each new thing.
consent.care: The legal age differs from place to place, so that answer has to come from a local source rather than from me. If something happened without your consent, that is not your fault, and there is support available through this app's healthcare portals and from a helpline.

contraception.answer: Contraception is anything used to prevent a pregnancy. It is not the same as protection from sexually transmitted infections, and methods differ in how well they do each.
contraception.detail: Some methods are used every time sex happens, such as condoms, and others are used once and then work for weeks or years, such as an implant or an IUD. Effectiveness varies a lot between methods, and between perfect use and real life, so it is worth asking about the numbers rather than guessing them.
contraception.care: The right method depends on whether pregnancy is the concern, whether infection protection is wanted, your health history, and whether you plan to have children later. A doctor or a family planning clinic can go through the options with you.

condoms.answer: A condom is a thin sheath put on before sex. It is the only method that both reduces the chance of pregnancy and greatly reduces the chance of passing on an STI.
condoms.detail: Condoms are used from the start of sex to the end, because sperm can be present before ejaculation. They are single use, and oil-based lubricant can weaken latex, which is worth checking on the pack.

sti.answer: STIs are infections that are passed through sexual contact. There are several of them, and they are not all passed the same way or at the same rates.
sti.detail: Many have no symptoms at all, particularly early on, so the absence of symptoms is not a reason to think you are in the clear. They are common, and they are treatable.
sti.warning: If you have had unprotected sex and there is any chance of an infection, get tested rather than waiting to see whether something appears.
sti.care: Testing is usually a swab or a blood sample, and results often come back within days. Most STIs are curable, and the earlier they are treated the simpler that treatment is.

painDuringSex.answer: Pain during sex is common, and it is never something to simply put up with. It has a number of possible causes, and it is often treatable.
painDuringSex.detail: Causes include dryness, an infection such as a UTI or thrush, endometriosis or fibroids, a condition affecting the skin of the vulva, and tension during penetration. Pain can also follow a previous difficult experience, and that is a real cause rather than a reason it is imagined.
painDuringSex.warning: Pain with bleeding after sex, pain with a fever, pain that is getting worse, or deep pain during or after sex should be seen by a doctor.
painDuringSex.care: A doctor or a gynaecologist can find the cause and treat it, including treating an infection, managing a condition, or helping with dryness and pain at penetration. Pelvic floor physiotherapy is a real option for some people, and so is reviewing contraception if that is involved.

lubrication.answer: The vagina produces moisture, and arousal increases it, but the amount varies a lot between people and from moment to moment. Less moisture than usual is common with stress, hormonal contraception, some medicines, and as menopause approaches.

pregnancyDuringPeriod.answer: Yes, you can get pregnant during a period, but it is not the most likely time to. Ovulation usually happens about two weeks before the next period starts, so the bleeding usually comes well after ovulation.
pregnancyDuringPeriod.detail: Cycle length differs between people, and ovulation does not always land in the same place within a cycle, particularly in shorter or irregular cycles. Sperm can also survive for several days, so a pregnancy can follow sex that happened days earlier. So the honest answer is that it is unlikely but not impossible.
pregnancyDuringPeriod.care: If avoiding pregnancy matters, do not rely on timing it around a period. If your cycles are irregular or short, a clinician can help you choose a reliable method.

pregnancyTest.answer: A home pregnancy test detects a hormone that appears once a pregnancy has started and builds up gradually. Testing too early is the most common reason for a negative result when a pregnancy is in fact present.
pregnancyTest.detail: A test taken on the first day of a missed period is more likely to be accurate than one taken earlier, and repeating a test after a few days can settle the question. Instructions matter too, so read how long to hold it and when to read the result window.

implantation.answer: Implantation is when a fertilised egg attaches to the uterine lining and settles into it. It happens about a week or two after fertilisation, roughly when a period would have been due.

miscarriage.answer: A miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy before it is far enough along to survive outside the body. It is unfortunately very common in early pregnancy, and it usually happens for reasons that are nobody's fault.
miscarriage.detail: Most early miscarriages are caused by a chromosome problem in the fertilised egg, which is a chance event. Stress, activity and food do not usually cause it, which matters, because a lot of people believe they caused theirs.
miscarriage.warning: Heavy bleeding, severe pain on one side, or pain with shoulder-tip pain and dizziness need urgent care, because those can mean something other than a straightforward miscarriage.
miscarriage.care: After a miscarriage you should be offered both physical aftercare and emotional support, and most people do better with both. When to try again is better decided once you feel ready, with a clinician's advice.

ectopicPregnancy.answer: An ectopic pregnancy is one that has started developing outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube. It cannot continue safely, and it has to be treated.
ectopicPregnancy.warning: One-sided pain with any bleeding in early pregnancy, especially with shoulder-tip pain, faintness or dizziness, needs emergency care rather than waiting.
ectopicPregnancy.care: A positive early pregnancy test alongside one-sided pain is treated urgently, usually with surgery or an injection depending on the situation. Acting quickly is what protects the other tube, and future pregnancies with it.

postpartum.answer: The postpartum period is the time after a birth, and it lasts about six weeks. Periods usually return somewhere between two and six months after the birth, and later than that if you are breastfeeding.
postpartum.detail: Breastfeeding can delay a period for longer, but it is still possible to conceive before your first period comes back, so contraception is worth discussing before that point.
postpartum.care: Bleeding or pain that continues past the early weeks, or anything that worries you, should be raised with a clinician at the postnatal visit rather than waited out.

pcos.answer: PCOS, polycystic ovary syndrome, is a common hormonal condition in which the ovaries release eggs irregularly and produce more androgens than usual.
pcos.detail: It is diagnosed from a combination of signs rather than one test: irregular or infrequent periods, signs of higher androgens such as acne or excess hair, and the appearance of the ovaries on an ultrasound. Body weight is often involved because the condition is linked to how the body handles insulin, but it says nothing about anybody's character, and it can happen at any body size.
pcos.warning: Periods that stop for months, heavy or prolonged bleeding, and difficulty conceiving are all reasons to be assessed rather than waited out.
pcos.care: Treatment follows the symptom rather than the name: irregular periods are often managed with the combined pill, fertility treatment when conception is wanted, and help with insulin resistance where it is present. Lifestyle changes help, and they are not a judgement on how anyone lives.

endometriosis.answer: Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows elsewhere in the body, most often on the ovaries, the fallopian tubes and the tissue lining the pelvis. It is a real, recognised condition, not a psychological complaint.
endometriosis.detail: It often causes period pain that gets worse over time, pain during sex, pain on passing urine or opening your bowels around periods, and difficulty conceiving. It takes a long time to diagnose because the symptoms overlap with many other conditions, so being told for years that the pain is normal is a recognised problem.
endometriosis.warning: Pain that is getting worse month on month, pain that stops you working, or heavy bleeding with a feeling of fullness should be taken seriously rather than adapted to.
endometriosis.care: There are treatments that reduce the pain, including hormonal ones, anti-inflammatory medicines, and surgery for some people. A gynaecologist who deals with endometriosis regularly makes a real difference to how quickly it is found.

fibroids.answer: Fibroids are growths in the muscle of the uterus. They are extremely common and are not cancerous, and many cause no symptoms at all.
fibroids.detail: When they do cause symptoms, the usual ones are heavy or prolonged periods, a feeling of pressure low in the abdomen, and needing to pass urine more often. They are found on an ultrasound.
fibroids.warning: Sudden one-sided pain, feeling faint alongside heavy bleeding, or periods that become suddenly and noticeably heavier are not things to wait out.
fibroids.care: Most fibroids need nothing beyond monitoring. When they cause trouble, treatment ranges from medicine that reduces bleeding to procedures that shrink or remove them, and the choice depends on age, symptoms and whether children are planned.

ovarianCysts.answer: An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled pocket in or on an ovary. The majority are common, harmless and cause no symptoms, and many disappear on their own.
ovarianCysts.detail: They are often found incidentally, on an ultrasound done for something else. A cyst that looks unusual on a scan, is large, or comes with pain is followed up rather than simply watched.
ovarianCysts.warning: Sudden severe one-sided pain, pain with vomiting or a fever, or pain with fainting needs urgent assessment rather than a routine appointment.
ovarianCysts.care: A doctor will usually repeat an ultrasound after a short interval, and check for pregnancy where that could explain it. Most need no treatment at all, some are monitored, and a small number need surgery.

thyroid.answer: A thyroid problem means the thyroid gland in the neck is making too much or too little hormone. It is common, it is easily missed, and it is treatable.
thyroid.detail: An underactive thyroid often brings heavy and irregular periods, tiredness, weight gain, dry skin and feeling cold. An overactive thyroid brings lighter periods, feeling hot, tremor, weight loss and anxiety. A simple blood test checks for it.
thyroid.warning: Periods that become very heavy or stop for months, alongside tiredness, unexplained weight change, or feeling unusually cold or hot, should be tested.
thyroid.care: A blood test for thyroid function, plus a thyroid-specific antibody test where it is relevant, is the starting point. Treatment is a daily tablet in both directions and it is usually lifelong, so a clinician should go through it with you.

anaemia.answer: Anaemia is a shortage of haemoglobin, the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen. It makes most people tired and low on energy, and it is very common in women with heavy periods.
anaemia.detail: Heavy bleeding can cause it over time, and so can too little iron in the diet, pregnancy, illness and some conditions. It is found with a simple blood test rather than by how you feel, which is why testing matters.
anaemia.care: Iron is the usual treatment when iron is low, and the type matters, because the tablets people often buy for themselves are poorly absorbed. It is worth having the cause checked too, particularly if periods are heavy, and re-testing after a course.

pelvicPain.answer: Pelvic pain is pain in the lower abdomen, below the navel, usually between the hips. It has many causes, including period cramps, infections, endometriosis, fibroids, ovarian cysts, constipation, urinary problems and strain.
pelvicPain.detail: What matters most is whether the pain is new, whether it is getting worse, whether it is one-sided, and whether it comes with a fever, bleeding or vomiting, because those narrow the causes down quickly.
pelvicPain.warning: Severe one-sided pain, pelvic pain with a fever, pain with vomiting, or pain with fainting or bleeding needs same-day care rather than a routine appointment.
pelvicPain.care: A doctor will usually examine you and may arrange tests depending on what they find. Pelvic floor physiotherapy is genuinely effective for a large share of chronic pelvic pain, and it is often the part people do not know exists.

uti.answer: A UTI is a urinary tract infection, most commonly a bacterial infection of the bladder. It is much more common in women, and it usually causes burning when you pass urine and a frequent urge to go.
uti.detail: It is not the same as a vaginal infection, even though the symptoms can feel similar, and the two need different treatment. Antibiotics usually work well, which is why a proper assessment matters.
uti.warning: A fever, pain in your back or side, vomiting, or symptoms that keep returning need medical attention, because a UTI that has reached the kidneys is more serious.
uti.care: A urine sample is usually the test. Drinking enough water and not holding urine for long can help prevent repeats, and women who get frequent UTIs sometimes need a different approach agreed with a doctor.

yeastInfection.answer: A yeast infection, or thrush, is an overgrowth of candida that most often affects the vagina. It causes itching, soreness and a thick discharge, and it is common.
yeastInfection.detail: It is not the same as bacterial vaginosis, which has a different smell and a different treatment, and confusing the two is why a lot of people end up treating an infection that has not gone away. Antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy, and damp or tight clothing can all encourage it.
yeastInfection.warning: Itching that keeps coming back, or itching and discharge that do not settle with treatment, needs an examination rather than more over-the-counter creams.
yeastInfection.care: An antifungal cream or pessary usually works, and a doctor can confirm the cause if it keeps recurring. Avoid douching and fragranced washes, which irritate the skin and make it worse.

pid.answer: PID, pelvic inflammatory disease, is an infection of the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries, most often following an untreated STI such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea.
pid.detail: It often causes pain low in the abdomen, pain during sex, unusual or heavy bleeding, and sometimes a fever, though it can be nearly silent. It is one of the main causes of tubal damage and later difficulty conceiving, which is why it is treated seriously.
pid.warning: Pelvic pain with a fever, pain with vomiting, or feeling unwell alongside abnormal bleeding needs same-day medical attention.
pid.care: Antibiotics treat it, and both partners are generally treated at the same time so that it is not passed back and forth. Being tested after unprotected sex with a new partner is the surest way to prevent it.

menopauseStages.answer: Menopause is the point at which a full year has passed without a period. It is a stage of life rather than an illness, and the years leading up to it are called perimenopause. Periods usually stop gradually, and bleeding for longer than a year afterwards should be checked.

perimenopause.answer: Perimenopause is the stage before menopause, when the body is changing and periods become less predictable. It usually begins in your forties and can last several years.
perimenopause.detail: Cycles often shorten, lengthen or become irregular, and symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats, disrupted sleep, mood changes and brain fog can appear. It is still possible to conceive in this stage, because ovulation does not stop all at once.
perimenopause.warning: Bleeding that is heavy across several cycles, bleeding between periods, or bleeding long after a full year without any, should be checked rather than assumed to be menopause.
perimenopause.care: None of these symptoms has to be endured unasked. Treatments for hot flushes, sleep problems and low mood are available, and HRT is one option among others that a clinician can weigh up with you, against your own health history.

hormonalContraceptives.answer: Some hormonal methods make periods much lighter, irregular, or stop them altogether. That is often what they do, and it is not a sign that something is wrong.
hormonalContraceptives.detail: It also means a stretch without any bleeding is no longer a reliable sign that you are not pregnant, which is worth knowing before assuming it. The pill, the implant, the injection and the hormonal IUD can all do this, in different ways.
hormonalContraceptives.care: A doctor can help work out whether a change in bleeding is a side effect to expect, a side effect to report, or a reason to change method. A new pattern that appears on a method you have used for years is worth mentioning rather than putting up with.

periodBlood.answer: Period blood is not dirty and not toxic. It is ordinary blood and uterine tissue, and the old idea that it carries waste is wrong.
periodBlood.detail: It can be darker brown, almost black, or thick, which happens when blood has been exposed to air and has had time to oxidise. The colour changes with the flow and is not a sign of illness. It may smell a little different, and any change that persists alongside itching, pain or a strong smell is worth having checked.

tamponMyths.answer: Tampons do not contain toxins, and they were never banned for being unhygienic. They are regulated and sold legally in most places.
tamponMyths.detail: The real caution is about how long one is left in. Staying in place much longer than its time limit very rarely lets bacteria grow and cause toxic shock syndrome, so the risk is low and it is about time, not about tampons being toxic.

virginityMyth.answer: There is no reliable way to tell whether somebody has had sex, and virginity is not something a body can prove. The hymen is a shape that varies from person to person and can change for reasons that have nothing to do with sex, such as exercise or stretching.
virginityMyth.detail: Nobody can tell from a single physical sign, and anyone who claims otherwise is guessing. Being believed about your own body is what matters.

sharkMyth.answer: Period blood does not attract sharks, and there is no reliable evidence that swimming while you are on a period is dangerous.

exerciseMyth.answer: Exercise does not stop your period by itself. Periods change when your energy intake, your stress or your routine changes, and very hard training combined with eating little can affect them.
exerciseMyth.detail: So the link is usually not exercise as such, but what the training does to your intake and your routine. Moderate exercise during a period is not a problem for most people; you may prefer a lighter session, and that is a preference rather than a medical rule.

firstTimeMyth.answer: Sex is not supposed to hurt the first time, and pain that does not settle afterwards is not something to expect or accept. Some people feel no discomfort at all, and many feel a small amount.
firstTimeMyth.detail: Pain that is sharp, severe, or that leaves you sore afterwards usually means something specific is happening: not enough arousal or moisture, a tight muscle, an infection, or a condition such as endometriosis. Those are all treatable. Bleeding is not a reliable marker of what happened before, so it is not evidence of anything.

emergencyQuestion.answer: You do not need me to tell you whether it is an emergency. A rule you can trust is this: if it is sudden, severe, getting worse, or it frightens you, get it seen today rather than waiting to see whether it settles.
emergencyQuestion.detail: Call emergency services straight away for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, severe bleeding, a possible fracture or a bad injury. Go to urgent care the same day for pain that is severe and new, a fever alongside pelvic pain, or anything that is not improving.

redFlagPeriodPain.answer: Period pain that is severe enough to stop you moving, working or sleeping, or that is much worse than it has been before, is not ordinary cramps and should be assessed.
redFlagPeriodPain.warning: Period pain with a fever, with vomiting, with fainting, or that is severe on one side only needs medical attention the same day.
redFlagPeriodPain.care: A doctor can look for the causes that are treatable, such as endometriosis, fibroids, adenomyosis, an infection, or an IUD in place. Pain that is worsening cycle after cycle deserves an answer rather than a stronger painkiller.

redFlagHeavyBleeding.answer: Bleeding that soaks a pad or a tampon every hour for more than an hour, or that leaves you dizzy, weak or faint, needs medical attention.
redFlagHeavyBleeding.warning: Bleeding that heavy alongside dizziness, palpitations, breathlessness or fainting is an emergency, and clots larger than a coin together with fainting need emergency care too.
redFlagHeavyBleeding.care: A doctor can check for anaemia and for the cause of the bleeding, and there are treatments that reduce it. Do not plan to manage heavy bleeding on your own while it is going on.

redFlagFainting.answer: Fainting, chest pain with breathlessness, a racing heart with dizziness, or weakness down one side of your body are not period symptoms, and they need emergency care.
redFlagFainting.warning: Call emergency services for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or sudden weakness or slurred speech. If it is new and there is no chest pain, get it seen the same day.
redFlagFainting.care: Anaemia caused by heavy bleeding is a common and treatable explanation for light-headedness, and it is worth ruling out. Anything involving the chest, breathing or one-sided weakness is an emergency rather than something to wait out.

redFlagPregnancy.answer: Bleeding or pain during a pregnancy needs checking. Pain on one side of the lower belly, bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, or a severe headache with changes in vision all need urgent assessment.
redFlagPregnancy.warning: One-sided pain with bleeding in early pregnancy is a medical emergency, because it can be an ectopic pregnancy. A severe headache, blurred vision or sudden swelling in pregnancy needs the same day care.
redFlagPregnancy.care: Contact a doctor or a maternity unit the same day for bleeding or pain in pregnancy. Where an ectopic pregnancy is possible, early review matters, because waiting can cost the other fallopian tube as well as the pregnancy.

redFlagAllergicReaction.answer: A severe allergic reaction is an emergency. Swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, widespread hives alongside breathing trouble, or feeling faint after an exposure should all be treated as anaphylaxis.
redFlagAllergicReaction.warning: Call emergency services for a throat that is closing, trouble breathing, or a reaction involving swelling or dizziness. Do not wait to see whether it passes.
redFlagAllergicReaction.care: If you have had a severe reaction before, ask a doctor whether you should carry an adrenaline auto-injector, and make sure anyone you live with knows where it is and how to use it.

badge.label: Anonymous
badge.explanation: Members are shown a random alias such as “Anonymous User #4821”. Your name and email are never shown next to anything you post.

identity.title: You are anonymous here
identity.body: Your alias is random and unrelated to your account. Nothing you post is connected to your cycle, symptoms or any other health record.

privacy.note: Posts are anonymous and are not linked to your health log. Do not share identifying details about yourself or anyone else.

composer.heading: Share something
composer.label: Write a post
composer.placeholder: You do not have to use your name, or anyone else’s.

feed.emptyBody: Be the first to post. Your name will not be shown.

report.title: Report
report.intro: Tell us what is wrong with the post by {author}. A person will read this.
report.anonymityNote: The person you report is not told who reported them. Please do not include your name in the details.

toast.blocked: You will no longer see posts by {author}.
toast.reported: Thank you. A person will read your report.

auth.gateTitle: Sign in to join the conversation
auth.gateBody: SecretChat is anonymous, but it still needs an account so replies have an author and abuse can be stopped. Your email is used to sign in and for nothing else — it is never shown next to anything you post.
auth.invalidCredentials: That email and password do not match an account.
auth.emailInUse: An account already exists for that email address.

setup.title: SecretChat is not connected yet
setup.body: A person who installs this app has to connect it to their own Supabase project first. Until then nothing here is sent or stored anywhere.
setup.noLocalStorage: Nothing from this page is saved on this device, and nothing from your health log can reach it.

identity.title: You are anonymous here, and so is everyone else
identity.body: Your feed shows a random alias and nothing that identifies you. You cannot be searched, and nothing from your health log can reach this page. Signing out ends this alias for good — a new one is issued the next time you return.

errors.invalid_request: That request was not valid. Check the form and try again.
errors.unauthenticated: Your session has ended. Sign in again to continue.
errors.not_configured: SecretChat is not connected to a database yet. An administrator needs to finish setup.
errors.upstream_unavailable: We could not reach the community right now. Try again in a moment.
errors.rate_limited: Too many actions at once. Wait a moment and try again.
